analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal greenhouse gas rules until China, India, and Russia adopt similar cuts.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had only two cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a committee or floor vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited the EPA and every other federal agency from issuing or enforcing any rule that reduces carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gas emissions until three officials certify in writing that China, India, and Russia have adopted and are enforcing substantially similar reductions. It also would have immediately wiped out any existing federal rule requiring emissions cuts, with no effective date tied to when that certification might happen.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and gas producers and energy-intensive manufacturers would gain the most: they would be freed indefinitely from federal carbon limits and from compliance costs on existing rules. Electric utilities relying on fossil fuels and consumers of energy-intensive products would also see costs deferred, at the price of continued emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the EPA and the head of any federal agency from implementing or enforcing any regulation, proposal, or action establishing carbon dioxide or greenhouse gas emissions reductions until China, India, and Russia have proposed, implemented, and enforced substantially similar reductions. [S2] [S3]
It goes further than a freeze: any existing regulation requiring emissions reductions would be declared to have no force or effect until the certification is made. [S2] [S3]

The bill's findings invoke the 1997 Byrd-Hagel resolution, in which the Senate said it would not accept climate commitments for developed countries unless developing countries faced the same commitments in the same period. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the costs of unchecked carbon emissions, including health effects from air pollution and long-term climate damage, while getting no federal reduction policy in return. Because the certification condition requires three foreign governments to adopt 'substantially similar' rules, the freeze could last indefinitely.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The bill would repeal existing emissions rules outright rather than waiting, so even current reductions requirements would stop applying the day it took effect, with no domestic backstop. [S2] [S3]

Supporters' own argument, stated in the bill's findings, is that unilateral U.S. carbon regulation puts the country at a competitive disadvantage while China, India, and Russia impose no similar rules; an honest reading is that the bill trades that claimed advantage for allowing domestic emissions to continue unregulated indefinitely. [S3]

The certification standard leaves the timing entirely outside U.S. control, since officials must certify that foreign governments have implemented and enforced 'substantially similar' reductions before any American rule can take effect. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real benefits to fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive industries in the form of avoided compliance costs, but it did so by eliminating all federal greenhouse gas regulation, including rules already in effect, with no end date that the U.S. government itself controlled. For the public, the bill's costs, continued emissions with no federal reduction policy, would fall on households through pollution exposure and long-term climate impacts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter introduced the bill on January 28, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works. [S5] [S1]
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Republicans. [S4]
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, and it never received a vote in the Senate or House before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the public avoided the loss of existing federal greenhouse gas rules and the indefinite regulatory freeze the bill would have imposed. Fossil fuel producers, who would have been the bill's main beneficiaries, gained nothing from its failure to advance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, since the bill never advanced

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled it for consideration; no action was taken after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All of the bill's support came from Republicans: its sponsor and two Republican cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsor on record, and no vote was ever taken. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would have repealed existing carbon rules and barred new ones indefinitely, relieving coal plants of emissions compliance costs. The public would pay through continued pollution and climate damage that the rules were designed to limit. [S2] [S3]
Greenhouse gas rules cover emissions from oil and gas operations and transportation fuels; freezing all such rules would preserve those producers' ability to emit without restriction. [S2]
These industries would avoid the energy and compliance costs of carbon regulation, a gain that comes at the public's expense in the form of continued emissions. [S3]
By nullifying emissions-reduction rules, the bill would remove the policy pressure that drives demand for wind, solar, and efficiency technologies, weakening their competitors in fossil energy. [S2]
